state.misconception_label: Does not understand that 2n represents an even number

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: Which of these shows part of the proof that the sum of two odd numbers is even? I got \( \begin{array}{l}2 n+(2 m+1) \\ =2(n+m)+1\end{array} \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think of it this way: Imagine you have 2 bags of marbles, each with an odd number of marbles. When you add them together, you combine all the marbles into one big bag. The total number of marbles in the big bag will be even because each individual bag had an odd number of marbles. So, in math terms, 2n represents an even number because it is the sum of two odd numbers.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh, I think I get it now - so 2n is even because it's like two groups of something? But wait, I'm confused about the marbles thing... if each bag has an odd number, how does that make it even when you put them together? And what does the "n" and "m" actually stand for in the original problem?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think of it like this: imagine you have two groups of friends, each with an odd number of people. When you combine both groups, the total number of friends will be even because each group started with an odd number. In the math problem, "n" and "m" are just placeholders for any number, so you can think of them as the number of friends in each group.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher provides mathematically incorrect explanations (claiming 2n is even because it's the sum of two odd numbers, and that combining two odd groups gives an even total), fails to address the student's actual misconception about algebraic representation, and the student's final turn shows increased confusion rather than improvement.
score.justification_pass2: While the teacher attempts to use concrete analogies (marbles, friends), the analogies are mathematically incorrect and confusing—claiming that adding two odd numbers gives an even number because 2n is even fundamentally misrepresents the proof structure, undermining the experiential approach rather than grounding it properly.
